HEALTHCARE DATA & AI-ASSISTED ANALYTICS

Atlas

Ask a question.
See the reasoning.

I integrated and standardized healthcare datasets with Python and Pandas, documented their meaning, and checked AI-assisted findings against the data and business rules. Atlas brings that work into a hospital analytics assistant, turning everyday questions into grouped results with visible interpretation and validation notes.

Python / PandasData qualityConversational analyticsSemantic dictionaryValidation notes
Read the Atlas project story

University of Arkansas · May–August 2026

Goal

Make healthcare data easier to explore through plain-language questions, with clear definitions and evidence behind each answer.

My contribution

I integrated and standardized datasets with Python and Pandas, developed data dictionaries and metadata, and checked AI-assisted findings against the data and business rules. I documented data quality and analytical findings alongside that work.

Result

Atlas presents grouped hospital operations results with a semantic interpretation, validation notes, and the steps used to produce an answer. The demo shows insurance mix by site and service-line summaries of encounter counts, length of stay, and billed charges.

Watch the one-minute Atlas walkthrough ↗

What I learned

An answer needs more than a convincing summary: the meaning of the fields and the checks behind it must be visible. Billed charges are distinct from costs, and length-of-stay comparisons are descriptive. Atlas is an aggregate analytics demonstration; the recording does not independently establish accuracy or clinical performance.

Marketing Analytics | Prediction

UARK · Group 9 project

Hog Heaven campaign analytics

January–May 2026

Compared SAS models for an engagement-based membership campaign, balancing classification error with the usefulness of the targeting recommendation.

SASPredictive modelingExploratory analysis
Read project details

University of Arkansas · January–May 2026 · Group 9

Team: Aqela Faizy, Dalton Wisdom, and Jackson Jessup.

Goal

Prioritize membership-campaign outreach using engagement and purchase-history data. The team created a target from engagement scores: 0–2 for unlikely to purchase and 3–5 for likely to purchase.

My contribution

The written report attributes the product-interest visualizations and comparisons of gradient boosting, decision trees, and HP Forest to me. I examined predictor selection and how the models classified customers.

Result
Misclassification rate · lower is better
ModelRate
Default logistic regression25.87%
Decision tree, 2 branches / depth 622.22%
Ensemble: regression, neural network, tree22.71%
Regression followed by decision tree22.22%
Gradient boosting, 2 branches / depth 620.79%

Source: Group 9 Hog Heaven Presentation, slides 12 and 15. The selected gradient-boosting model has a 5.08 percentage-point lower error rate than the logistic baseline in that presentation.

The report records a separate gradient-boosting error rate of 21.86%. The files do not explain its difference from the presentation’s 20.79%, so the results remain labeled separately.

What I learned

Model quality depends on the target as well as the error rate. An engagement-based label is a proxy for purchase intent; these results do not establish actual campaign conversion or revenue gains.

Business Intelligence | Data Architecture

UARK · Team J project

County data warehouse & BI

January–May 2026

Integrated county-level property, crime, demographic, and economic data into a dimensional warehouse for analytical reporting.

SQL ServerETLDimensional modeling
Read project details

University of Arkansas · January–May 2026 · Team J

Team: Ben Boyle, Dalton Wisdom, Jackson Jessup, and Vaishnavi Vanteru.

Goal

Explore county-level property values alongside crime, demographic, and economic indicators.

My contribution

I worked with Team J on this data warehouse and business intelligence project. The schema and reports shown here are shared team deliverables.

Our implementation connected property data from Zillow and Realtor, Census data, and FBI NIBRS records through shared county and date dimensions. The presentation describes 721,453 incident records from 2020–2023 and a load combining 12 crime CSVs.

Result

A dimensional warehouse and report examples supported comparisons of affordability, market liquidity, and county indicators.

What I learned

Consistent geography, time periods, and field definitions determine whether joined data is useful. Limited recent Census and property data and voluntary NIBRS reporting affect interpretation; county-level associations do not establish causation or predict an individual decision.

Personal Projects

Putting my ideas into practice: ChemAtlas connects science with software, and Course Hub brings my learning workflow together.

WHERE SCIENCE MEETS SOFTWARE

ChemAtlas

Big ideas.
Meet hands-on learning.

Drawing on my biochemistry background, I am developing a learning platform that brings explanations, interactive molecular geometry, and practice tools together.

JavaScriptCanvasHTML / CSSVercel
Explore ChemAtlas ↗View source ↗
Read ChemAtlas project story
Goal

Help learners connect chemistry explanations with molecular models and opportunities to practice.

My contribution

I set the curriculum direction and used AI-assisted implementation to build learning material and interactive tools. General Chemistry provides the foundation for later topics, with explanations, worked examples, and practice kept close together.

Result

ChemAtlas brings learning modules, molecular geometry, and practice tools into one developing platform. Its repository includes General Chemistry modules, practice engines, Organic Chemistry tools, and a tutor implementation. A guest-first experience lets visitors explore before creating an account.

What I learned

Interaction needs a clear learning purpose. Connecting a concept with a model or an activity is the design goal; observing learners is the next step. Curriculum and cloud features are evolving, and learning gains have not been formally measured.

A LITTLE MORE ORGANIZED

Course Hub

Less searching.
More doing.

I developed a workspace to organize two graduate courses, source documents, meeting notes, assignments, and AI-assisted writing. The focus is a clear path through each week's work.

Next.jsSupabaseOpenAIPython
Read Course Hub project story
Goal

Keep readings, transcripts, meeting notes, assignments, and drafts together in a clear weekly learning workflow.

My contribution

I defined the workflows, directed AI-assisted implementation, and refined the Hub through everyday coursework. I requested focused writing prompts, revisions that retain my edits, and visible loading states to prevent duplicate submissions.

Result

A personal workspace for two graduate courses, organized around Announcement → Content → Assignment. The Weekly Snapshot brings both courses and assignment counts together, while uploaded sources support meeting notes and AI-assisted writing.

The web app is deployed for personal use and continues to evolve. AI features and heavy-file processing depend on server configuration; the portfolio shows the interface without opening access to private coursework.

What I learned

Using the tool exposed practical problems with uploads, overlapping inputs, and unclear button feedback. Those issues guided the next changes. A useful AI writing workflow preserves the writer’s choices and makes each action’s status clear.

What connects it all

Accurate information, clear documentation, and thoughtful testing — from the lab bench to the systems I build.
